questions.question: Define Stress. Discuss the neural axes of stress response. / [CO1, CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Define Stress. Discuss the neural axes of stress response. / [CO1, CO2]
  • Ans: Stress is the nonspecific response of the body to any demand made upon it. It is a “fight or
  • flight” response intended to do—to prepare you to fight or to flee from a life-threatening event.
  • The body’s fastest stress response comes from the neural system, which includes the sympathetic
  • nervous system (SNS) and the parasympathetic nervous system (PNS), both part of the
  • autonomic nervous system (ANS). These systems send signals through neurotransmitters to
  • organs, muscles, and the brain. The SNS activates the fight-or-flight response: it increases heart
  • rate, dilates pupils, diverts blood to large muscles, and releases glucose for energy, while
  • reducing digestion. The PNS activates the rest-and-digest response: it slows the heart rate and
  • reactivates digestion once the threat is gone. However, too much SNS activation relies on
  • primitive brain functions and suppresses higher-order thinking in the front brain. This is called
  • cortical inhibition, where problem-solving and clear thinking are impaired. This mental
  • confusion can further raise heart rate, creating a negative cycle.
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025

questions.question: Define panic disorder. Describe different disease, disorder and symptoms that are associated with it / [CO1, CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Define panic disorder. Describe different disease, disorder and symptoms that are associated
  • with it / [CO1, CO2]
  • Ans: The DSM-5 describes panic disorder as recurrent unexpected (i.e., no obvious cues or
  • triggers) panic attacks. Panic disorder is associated with psychiatric and physical comorbidity,
  • suicidal ideation and attempts, and overall decreased quality of life. Panic disorder was
  • significantly associated with cardiovascular diseases and peripheral vascular disease.
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025

questions.question: What is psychological triage in the context of mental health? / [CO2, CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• What is psychological triage in the context of mental health? / [CO2, CO3]
  • Ans: Psychological triage in mental health is the rapid assessment and sorting of people affected
  • by a crisis to decide who needs urgent psychological help first. It involves observing emotional
  • and behavioral signs (like crying, shouting, or freezing), identifying specific needs (such as
  • calming or emotional support), and prioritizing care based on severity. The goal is to provide
  • psychological first aid and support in the most effective and timely way, especially during
  • disasters or traumatic events.
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025

questions.question: Give two examples of professionals or agencies to whom a crisis worker might refer an individual for continued care / [CO2, CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• Give two examples of professionals or agencies to whom a crisis worker might refer an
  • individual for continued care / [CO2, CO3]
  • Ans: After providing immediate support, a crisis worker may refer individuals to various
  • professionals and agencies for continued care based on their needs. These include psychiatrists
  • for medication and management of severe mental health issues, clinical psychologists or
  • counselors for therapy and trauma recovery, and social workers who assist with emotional and
  • practical needs such as housing, welfare, or employment. Referrals may also be made to
  • psychiatric nurses for follow-up care, community mental health centers and NGOs for ongoing
  • counseling and rehabilitation, and support groups that provide peer encouragement and reduce
  • isolation. In cases of abuse or neglect, survivors may be linked to women’s shelters or child
  • protection services, while faith-based counselors and rehabilitation centers offer additional
  • emotional and physical recovery options. These coordinated referrals ensure that individuals
  • receive comprehensive, continuous, and holistic care addressing their psychological, medical,
  • and social well-being.
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025

questions.question: Describe types of loss / [CO1, CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Describe types of loss / [CO1, CO2]
  • Ans: Materialistic Losses: These are visible, measurable losses of things that people own or use.
  • Examples: Destruction of houses, roads, vehicles. Loss of crops, livestock, land. Death of
  • earning members (economic loss). Loss of job or business income.
  • Non-Materialistic Losses: These are intangible, emotional, and social losses that cannot be
  • easily measured. Examples: Grief, trauma, fear, and loss of self-confidence. Separation from
  • family or community. Breakdown of social and cultural practices. Loss of faith, trust, or sense of
  • security.
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025

questions.question: Discuss how the use of mood-altering substances can affect emergency responders after trauma. / [CO1, CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Discuss how the use of mood-altering substances can affect emergency responders after
  • trauma. / [CO1, CO2]
  • Ans: People use a wide variety of both legal and illegal mood-altering substances in the wake of
  • disaster, trauma, and general adversity. It’s a form of self medication designed to lessen the
  • negative impact of the adversity. When PFA providers are working with emergency responders,
  • it’s also important to inquire not only about the use of alcohol but about energy drinks. Energy
  • drinks are sympathomimetic stimulants capable of inducing generalized, potentially excessive
  • arousal. Sleep disturbance, anxiety, difficulty concentrating, tachycardia, and arrhythmias are
  • possible consequences of overuse.
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025

questions.question: Differentiate between fear and anxiety / [CO1, CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Differentiate between fear and anxiety / [CO1, CO2]
  • Ans: Fear is stimulus specific, causing arousal and apprehension—a fear of snakes, for example.
  • Anxiety is generalized apprehension and arousal, free floating and less associated with a highly
  • defined specific stimulus. When the source of danger is obvious, the experienced emotion has
  • been called fear (e.g., “I’m afraid of snakes”). With anxiety, however, we frequently cannot
  • specify clearly what the danger is (e.g., “I’m anxious about my parents’ health”). Fear or panic is
  • a basic emotion that involves activation of the fight-or-flight response of the autonomic nervous
  • system; it occurs in response to imminent danger. Anxiety is a more diffuse blend of emotions
  • that includes high levels of negative affect, worry about possible threat or danger, and the sense
  • of being unable to predict threat or to control it if it occurs.
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025

questions.question: What is supportive communication in PFA? / [CO2, CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• What is supportive communication in PFA? / [CO2, CO3]
  • Ans: Supportive communication in PFA refers to expressing care and understanding through
  • respectful words, gentle tone, and nonverbal behaviors such as nodding and open body language.
  • It involves being patient, validating the person’s feelings, and offering comfort without
  • judgment. This type of communication helps individuals feel heard, valued, and emotionally
  • secure during a crisis.

questions.question: How does prioritization in the RAPID Model help mitigate distress in a multi-casualty scenario? / [CO2, CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• How does prioritization in the RAPID Model help mitigate distress in a multi-casualty
  • scenario? / [CO2, CO3]
  • Ans: In a multi-casualty scenario, prioritization in the RAPID Model helps mitigate distress by
  • enabling crisis workers to quickly identify and attend to individuals who are in the greatest
  • psychological need. Using psychological triage, responders assess emotional, behavioral, and
  • cognitive signs—such as panic, aggression, confusion, or dissociation—to determine who
  • requires immediate intervention. This process prevents chaos and ensures that those at the
  • highest risk of self-harm, severe distress, or endangering others receive prompt support. By
  • following a structured hierarchy of urgency, based on factors like severity of trauma, perceived
  • life threat, and prior psychiatric history, responders can stabilize the environment, reduce
  • emotional overload, and restore safety and order. Ultimately, prioritization ensures efficient use
  • of limited resources and facilitates quicker recovery for individuals and the larger affected
  • community by addressing the most critical needs first.
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025

questions.question: Describe recovery and adaptation needs / [CO1, CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Describe recovery and adaptation needs / [CO1, CO2]
  • Ans: Recovery needs: are those that help in coping with the loss and pain triggered by any
  • disaster. The healing process might take time and would be different for each individual.
  • Individual, group, and community level practices (cultural practices, rituals, group activities)
  • help in the healing process.
  • Adaptation needs: are the higher order needs for any disaster survivor. Building
  • psychosocial competencies among disaster survivors would yield post-traumatic growth –
  • adaptation, coping and resilience.

questions.question: Explain the difference between spiritual distress and dysfunction. / [CO2, CO3] [3x10 = 30]
questions.solution_html:
• Explain the difference between spiritual distress and dysfunction. / [CO2, CO3]
  • Ans: Spiritual distress refers to temporary questioning or struggle with one’s beliefs, often
  • triggered by challenging life events. Examples include questioning faith or questioning God’s
  • actions during a crisis. These experiences are usually reflective and do not stop the individual
  • from engaging in faith-related practices or rituals.
  • Spiritual dysfunction occurs when struggles with faith become persistent and impair
  • spiritual functioning. Examples include cessation of faith-related practices or projecting one’s
  • faith onto others in a way that disrupts relationships or community participation. Dysfunction
  • requires intervention, guidance, or counseling to help the person restore balance in their spiritual
  • life.
  • [3x10 = 30]

questions.question: The RAPID model is often used in Psychological First Aid. How would you use each step (Rapport, Assessment, Prioritization, Intervention, and Disposition) if you were helping someone after sexual abuse? / [CO4, CO5]
questions.solution_html:
• The RAPID model is often used in Psychological First Aid. How would you use each step
  • (Rapport, Assessment, Prioritization, Intervention, and Disposition) if you were helping someone
  • after sexual abuse? / [CO4, CO5]
  • Ans: In applying the RAPID model of Psychological First Aid after sexual abuse, the process
  • starts with Rapport,Rapport, where the helper offers empathy, active listening, and reassurance,
  • creating a safe, nonjudgmental space and validating the survivor by saying things like “I believe
  • you.” In Assessment, the helper gently checks the survivor’s emotional and physical state,
  • ensuring their immediate safety and identifying any need for medical care or signs of severe
  • distress or self-harm. Prioritization then helps determine what needs to be addressed first—such
  • as physical injury, safety concerns, or high emotional distress. During Intervention, the focus is
  • on calming and supporting the survivor through grounding techniques, normalizing their
  • reactions, and offering practical help that restores a sense of control. Finally, in Disposition, the
  • helper connects the survivor with ongoing support such as medical services, legal aid,
  • counseling, or trusted family members, and encourages follow-up to ensure continued care and
  • recovery.

questions.question: Evaluate the Essential Psychological Skills Required for Effective Psychological First Aid. / [CO4, CO5]
questions.solution_html:
• Evaluate the Essential Psychological Skills Required for Effective Psychological First Aid.
  • / [CO4, CO5]
  • Ans: Effective Psychological First Aid (PFA) requires a set of essential psychological skills that
  • enable helpers to support individuals in crisis with sensitivity, empathy, and professionalism.
  • One key skill is active and reflective listening, which helps the survivor feel heard, respected,
  • and understood without judgment or pressure to disclose more than they wish. Empathy is
  • crucial for conveying compassion and building trust, allowing the helper to connect emotionally
  • and validate the person’s experiences. Observation and assessment skills enable the helper to
  • recognize verbal and nonverbal signs of distress, identify immediate safety needs, and evaluate
  • the risk of harm or further trauma. Calm presence and emotional regulation are also vital, as the
  • helper must maintain composure and provide a sense of stability to the distressed individual.
  • Additionally, communication skills—using gentle tone, reassuring words, and culturally
  • sensitive language—promote comfort and trust. Problem-solving and decision-making skills help
  • in identifying priorities and linking survivors to appropriate medical, legal, and psychosocial
  • resources. Finally, empowerment and advocacy skills ensure that individuals regain a sense of
  • control, dignity, and hope. Together, these psychological skills form the foundation of effective
  • PFA, ensuring safety, emotional stabilization, and a pathway toward long-term recovery.
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025

questions.question: If you were the crisis interventionist in Matt’s role, how would you apply the appraisal step to Claire’s case and prioritize her needs after the flood? / [CO2, CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• If you were the crisis interventionist in Matt’s role, how would you apply the appraisal step
  • to Claire’s case and prioritize her needs after the flood? / [CO2, CO3]
  • Ans: If I were in Matt’s role, I would begin with appraisal to assess the severity of Claire’s
  • distress. She shows physiological (fatigue, disturbed sleep), cognitive (racing thoughts,
  • nightmares), and emotional (sadness, helplessness) indicia, suggesting distress but not
  • dysfunction. My first priority would be meeting her physical and safety needs by encouraging
  • rest, food, and hydration. Next, I would support her emotionally through reflective listening and
  • reassurance that her reactions are normal after trauma. I would then assess her cognitive
  • symptoms to ensure they don’t progress into dysfunction. Finally, I would strengthen her social
  • support system, encouraging connection with her caring neighbors to help her regain safety,
  • stability, and control.

  • loss. During disaster situations, caregivers play a crucial role in restoring safety, providing
